expandableCase.label: Applied classroom case
expandableCase.title: Bridging Home Language Strengths in Kindergarten Read-Alouds
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A kindergarten student from a Spanish-speaking home tracks print left-to-right during shared big-book reading and retells story sequences accurately in Spanish, yet gives one-word responses during English discussions and scores 6/20 on an English picture-naming check.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Pair interactive English read-alouds with visual story cards, home-language cognate bridges, and family storytelling prompts.
expandableCase.explanation: Visual response scaffolds and home-language bridges preserve grade-level comprehension while accelerating oral English vocabulary transfer and monitoring early growth. Moving the child to silent letter-copying drills overlooks strong narrative comprehension and deprives the learner of rich oral language input.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: In a K–2 literacy lesson, how should a elementary literacy teacher use a developmental literacy continuum?
choices: Use the continuum to anticipate prerequisites while assessing each learner, not treating stages as fixed gates.
Expect every learner to master each continuum skill at the same chronological age before moving to new instruction.
Skip foundational word-level evidence whenever comprehension appears weak, since higher skills reveal lower ones.
Use current grade placement as the main indicator of instructional need and select materials only from that level.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Literacy components develop in related and partly overlapping ways; a continuum organizes assessment and instruction but does not erase individual, linguistic, cultural, disability, or opportunity differences. The decision should remain tied to the assessed literacy skill, grade-appropriate text access, explicit instruction, and observable progress evidence.

chapterTakeaways: Oral language syntax, listening vocabulary, and narrative discourse form the foundation for K-6 reading comprehension under the Simple View of Reading and Scarborough's Rope.

expandableCase.label: Applied classroom case
expandableCase.title: Targeting Consonant-Blend Phoneme Segmentation in Kindergarten
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: Midyear screening shows four kindergarteners clap syllables and generate rhymes accurately, yet score 3/12 on phoneme segmentation fluency. They consistently drop the internal consonant in initial blends such as "slip" and "frog" and confuse spoken /m/ with /n/.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Form a brief Tier 2 group using Elkonin boxes, tactile counters, mirror articulatory cues, and letter tiles to map each phoneme.
expandableCase.explanation: Students who grasp syllables and rhyme but omit blend phonemes need explicit phonemic segmentation paired with articulatory feedback and graphemes for orthographic transfer. Repeating whole-class rhyming songs addresses an already mastered phonological level and misses the phoneme-level bottleneck.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: While planning explicit emergent-literacy instruction, how do phonological awareness and phonemic awareness differ?
choices: Phonemic awareness concerns the meanings of words, while phonological awareness concerns how sentences are built.
Phonological awareness spans spoken units such as syllables and rimes; phonemic awareness targets individual phonemes.
Both phonological and phonemic awareness require printed letters, so neither can be practiced through oral activities.
Phonics is the broader oral category, and phonological awareness is one narrower part of letter-sound instruction.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Phonological awareness includes words, syllables, onset-rime, and phonemes; phonemic awareness is the most specific level and can be practiced orally before or alongside graphemes. knowledgeChecks.prompt: While planning explicit emergent-literacy instruction, which task measures phoneme segmentation?
choices: Identifying the meaning of a morpheme within a word, such as explaining that un- in unhappy means not.
Combining a sequence of spoken phonemes into a whole word, such as hearing /s/ /u/ /n/ and saying sun.
Separating a spoken word into each of its individual phonemes, such as saying /m/ /a/ /p/ for map.
Naming each printed letter in a written word in order, such as reading the letters m, a, p aloud from a card.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Segmentation requires identifying the sequence of phonemes in a spoken word; the number of sounds need not equal the number of printed letters. chapterTakeaways: Phonological awareness progresses from words, syllables, and onset-rime down to individual phonemes; phonemic awareness focuses purely on spoken sounds before adding print letters.
Segmenting and blending individual phonemes have the strongest direct payoff for K-2 decoding and spelling, especially when students push Elkonin sound boxes and then map letters.
Concepts of print—book handling, left-to-right directionality, return sweep, and one-to-one voice-to-print matching—are assessed during shared reading and taught explicitly in context.

expandableCase.label: Applied classroom case
expandableCase.title: Replacing Picture Guessing with Explicit Long-Vowel Phonics
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: Six first graders decode CVC words at 95% accuracy but drop to 58% on a midyear phonics survey featuring VCe and vowel-team patterns. They read "cape" as "cap" and "boat" as "bot", frequently looking at illustrations to guess words in predictable leveled readers.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Regroup the students for explicit VCe and vowel-team lessons with cumulative review, word chaining, and matched decodable texts.
expandableCase.explanation: Systematic long-vowel instruction paired with decodable practice compels students to process internal vowel graphemes before bridging to authentic trade books. Keeping these readers in predictable leveled texts with picture-cueing prompts reinforces guessing habits instead of building reliable decoding.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right emergent literacy flow from receptive and expressive oral language through interactive read-alouds, concepts of print, and emergent writing to early progress checks and family partnerships.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, receptive and expressive oral language—including home-language vocabulary and syntax—establishes the foundation for reading development. Second, interactive read-alouds and dialogic talk routines expand academic language and scaffold oral retelling. Third, shared print engagement builds concepts of print such as book handling, directionality, and word boundaries. Fourth, alphabetic understanding and emergent writing connect letter names and speech sounds to early invented spelling. textEquivalent: Receptive and Expressive Oral Language: Listening comprehension, spoken vocabulary, syntax, and multilingual home-language assets form the primary language-to-literacy bridge for early K–6 learners.

Interactive Read-Alouds and Dialogic Talk: Teachers model expressive reading, ask open-ended prompts, expand student utterances, and scaffold oral retelling to strengthen narrative and academic language.

Concepts of Print and Shared Print Engagement: Shared big-book reading explicitly develops book handling, left-to-right return sweep, one-to-one word tracking, and the distinction between letters, words, and punctuation.

Alphabetic Principle and Emergent Writing: Connecting letter names and sounds to developmental drawing, labeling, and phonetic invented spelling moves children from print curiosity into early sound-symbol encoding.

Emergent Progress Checks and Family Partnership: Oral language samples, emergent behavior checklists, opportunity-to-learn reviews, visual response scaffolds, and home-language family partnerships inform responsive early instruction.

diagrams.title: Phonological Awareness to Phonemic Awareness & Orthographic Mapping Progression
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Trace how K–6 students progress from larger spoken units to phoneme-level blending, segmenting, and manipulation, then bond phonemes to graphemes for orthographic mapping.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow linking the spoken phonological continuum from word and syllable awareness through phonemic manipulation to phoneme–grapheme orthographic mapping.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right progression from word and syllable awareness through onset-rime and phoneme blending, segmenting, and manipulation to phoneme-grapheme orthographic mapping.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, students attend to larger spoken units by counting words in sentences and blending or segmenting syllables. Second, they notice intrasyllabic onset and rime boundaries through rhyming and onset-rime blending. Third, they build foundational phonemic awareness by isolating, blending, and segmenting individual phonemes. Fourth, they advance to phoneme deletion, addition, and substitution. Finally, pairing spoken phonemes with printed graphemes drives orthographic mapping so words are stored for effortless sight recognition.
textEquivalent: Word and Syllable Awareness: Students hear spoken sentence boundaries, count words, and blend or clap syllables in compound and multisyllabic words without requiring print.
Onset-Rime Sensitivity: Learners recognize rhymes, isolate initial consonant onsets from vowel-final rimes, and blend onset-rime chunks such as /s/ + /at/ into whole spoken words.
Phoneme Blending and Segmenting: Students isolate initial, final, and medial sounds, orally blend discrete phonemes into words, and segment spoken words into exact phoneme counts using sound boxes.
Phoneme Deletion and Substitution: Developing readers perform advanced phonemic manipulation by deleting, adding, or substituting target phonemes in initial, medial, final, and blend positions.

Phoneme-Grapheme Orthographic Mapping: Connecting segmented spoken phonemes directly to printed letters and letter patterns bonds pronunciation, spelling, and meaning into permanent sight-word memory.

nodes.label: Word & Syllable Awareness
nodes.detail: Early phonological awareness begins with large spoken units: tracking words in oral sentences, blending compound words, and counting or segmenting syllables.

nodes.label: Onset–Rime Sensitivity
nodes.detail: Students analyze intrasyllabic units by identifying rhymes, separating the initial consonant cluster (onset) from the vowel and coda (rime), and blending spoken onset–rime parts.

nodes.label: Phoneme Blending & Segmenting
nodes.detail: Core phonemic awareness isolates individual speech sounds, orally blends phonemes to read words, and segments spoken words into ordered phonemes using Elkonin sound boxes.

nodes.label: Phoneme Deletion & Substitution
nodes.detail: Advanced phonemic proficiency adds, deletes, and substitutes phonemes across single consonants and blends (for example, changing "slip" to "sip" or "slap") to sharpen sound-structure mastery.

nodes.label: Phoneme–Grapheme Orthographic Mapping
nodes.detail: Mapping each spoken phoneme to its exact printed grapheme anchors letter sequences to pronunciation and meaning, turning decoded words into instantly recognized sight words.

diagrams.title: Phoneme–Grapheme Mapping, Heart-Part Irregulars, & Phonics Error Analysis
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Apply synthetic phonics blending, heart-part irregular word analysis, decodable text practice, and nonsense-word error analysis to regroup elementary students for phonics mastery.
diagrams.caption: An original classroom phonics workflow connecting explicit phoneme–grapheme mapping and irregular heart-part routines to decodable application, diagnostic decoding surveys, and flexible skill regrouping.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right phonics workflow from explicit phoneme-grapheme mapping and heart-part irregular word instruction through decodable text application and phonics survey error analysis to skill regrouping.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, teachers explicitly map phonemes to graphemes across CVC, digraph, blend, VCe, vowel-team, and r-controlled patterns using synthetic blending. Second, teachers address partially irregular high-frequency words by mapping decodable letter-sound parts first and highlighting only the unexpected heart part. Third, students immediately practice cumulative patterns in decodable texts and dictated encoding. Fourth, brief phonics decoding surveys and nonsense-word probes expose specific grapheme-substitution patterns. Finally, teachers use mastery-rate data to regroup students for targeted reteaching and bridge smoothly to authentic elementary texts.
textEquivalent: Explicit Phoneme-Grapheme Mapping: Introduce target sound-spelling patterns (CVC, digraphs, blends, VCe, vowel teams, and r-controlled vowels) through explicit sound-to-letter mapping and continuous synthetic blending.

Irregular Word Heart-Part Instruction: Anchor high-frequency words with unexpected spellings by mapping all regular phoneme-grapheme correspondences first and explicitly teaching only the irregular grapheme part.
Decodable Text and Cumulative Review: Provide immediate connected reading in controlled decodable passages alongside cumulative review and word dictation so patterns stick reliably.

Phonics Survey and Nonsense-Word Error Analysis: Use targeted phonics decoding surveys, nonsense-word reading probes, and high-frequency inventories to diagnose specific grapheme-substitution errors without relying on picture guessing.

Small-Group Regrouping and Authentic Text Bridge: Track phonics mastery rates to form flexible skill-based groups for reteaching and guide proficient decoders from decodable passages into authentic grade-level books.

nodes.label: Explicit Phoneme–Grapheme Mapping
nodes.detail: Teach CVC, consonant digraph, blend, VCe, vowel-team, and r-controlled correspondences through sound-box mapping, orthographic routines, and continuous synthetic blending.

nodes.label: Irregular Word Heart-Part Analysis
nodes.detail: Teach temporarily or permanently irregular high-frequency words by mapping every predictable phoneme–grapheme match first and marking only the unexpected spelling part.

nodes.label: Decodable Text & Cumulative Review
nodes.detail: Pair new and previously taught patterns in connected decodable passages and dictated spelling to build accuracy before fading text control.

nodes.label: Phonics Survey & Nonsense-Word Audit
nodes.detail: Analyze phonics decoding surveys, nonsense-word probes, and high-frequency word inventories to isolate exact grapheme-substitution or vowel-pattern errors.

nodes.label: Skill Regrouping & Authentic Text Bridge
nodes.detail: Use phonics mastery-rate tracking to adjust small-group instruction promptly and bridge confident decoders into grade-level authentic literature and informational texts.

diagrams.title: Explicit Systematic Phonics & Multisyllabic Word-Analysis Sequence
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Organize K–6 systematic phonics instruction from closed-syllable CVC patterns through advanced vowel patterns, six syllable types, and affixes into connected decodable reading and encoding.
diagrams.caption: An original instructional sequence tracing explicit phonics progression from CVC words, digraphs, and blends through vowel patterns, six syllable types, and affixes to connected decodable transfer.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right phonics progression from CVC, digraphs, and blends through silent-e, vowel teams, and r-controlled vowels to six syllable types, common affixes, and connected decodable text transfer.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, explicit instruction establishes short-vowel CVC words, consonant digraphs, and consonant blends alongside continuous blending and spelling. Second, students master long-vowel silent-e (VCe), vowel teams, diphthongs, and r-controlled vowel patterns. Third, learners apply the six syllable types and flexible syllable-division strategies to decode longer words. Fourth, they analyze common inflectional and derivational affixes to read and spell multisyllabic words. Finally, cumulative practice in connected decodable text and dictated encoding secures accurate classroom transfer.
textEquivalent: Short-Vowel CVC, Digraphs, and Blends: Teachers introduce high-utility consonant-vowel correspondences, closed-syllable CVC blending, two-letter digraphs representing one sound (sh, ch, th), and adjacent consonant blends.

Silent-e, Vowel Teams, and R-Controlled Vowels: Systematic lessons build mastery of VCe long vowels, predictable vowel teams and diphthongs (ai, oa, oi), and r-controlled patterns (ar, er, ir, or, ur).
Six Syllable Types and Syllable Division: Students identify closed, open, VCe, vowel-team, r-controlled, and consonant-le syllables to break unfamiliar multisyllabic words into readable chunks.

Common Affixes and Structural Analysis: Learners peel off frequent prefixes (un-, re-, pre-) and suffixes (-ed, -ing, -ful, -tion) while checking spelling shifts and pronunciation changes in base words.

Connected Decodable Text and Encoding Transfer: Immediate reading of cumulative decodable passages paired with word chaining and sentence dictation transfers taught patterns from isolation to authentic print.

nodes.label: CVC, Digraphs & Blends
nodes.detail: Teach high-utility letter–sound correspondences in closed short-vowel CVC words first, then expand to single-sound digraphs (sh, th, ch, ck) and initial/final consonant blends.

nodes.label: Silent-e, Vowel Teams & R-Controlled
nodes.detail: Progress systematically to VCe long vowels, vowel teams and diphthongs (ee, ai, oa, ou, oy), and r-controlled vowels (ar, or, er, ir, ur) with explicit contrast sorts.

nodes.label: Six Syllable Types & Division
nodes.detail: Use closed, open, VCe, vowel-team, r-controlled, and consonant-le patterns with flexible vowel-spot division routines to decode unfamiliar multisyllabic words.

nodes.label: Common Affixes & Base Words
nodes.detail: Analyze inflectional endings (-s, -ed, -ing) and high-frequency prefixes/suffixes (re-, un-, dis-, -less, -ment) to chunk long words by meaning and sound.

nodes.label: Connected Decodable & Encoding Transfer
nodes.detail: Apply newly taught and review patterns immediately in controlled decodable texts, word chains, and dictated encoding so students rely on decoding rather than guessing.

diagrams.title: Vocabulary Depth, Morphology, and Academic Language Development
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Sequence robust elementary vocabulary instruction from high-utility Tier 2 word selection through morphological analysis and semantic networks to active oral and written use.
diagrams.caption: An original instructional flow illustrating how explicit Tier 2 selection, root-and-affix morphology, and rich semantic networks build transferable academic language.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right vocabulary development flow from explicit Tier 2 selection through morphological analysis and semantic networks to oral and written academic application.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the teacher selects high-utility Tier 2 academic words and central Tier 3 unit terms, introducing student-friendly explanations and accurate pronunciation. Second, students unpack roots, prefixes, and suffixes to generate related word families and leverage cross-linguistic cognates. Third, learners deepen meaning through semantic gradients, concept webs, examples, non-examples, and varied contexts. Finally, structured academic talk and writing prompts require students to apply new vocabulary accurately across subjects.
textEquivalent: Explicit Tier 2 Word Selection: Teachers prioritize high-utility academic words (Tier 2) essential to text comprehension alongside key domain concepts (Tier 3), teaching student-friendly definitions and pronunciation.

Morphological Analysis of Roots and Affixes: Students break target words into meaningful roots, prefixes, and suffixes, linking word families (for example, predict, prediction, unpredictable) and recognizing Spanish-English cognates.
Semantic Networks and Multiple Contexts: Learners map synonyms, antonyms, semantic gradients, examples, and non-examples across repeated encounters in read-alouds and informational texts.
Oral and Written Academic Application: Structured partner talk, sentence frames, and text-based writing prompt students to retrieve and use target vocabulary flexibly in new contexts.

nodes.label: Explicit Tier 2 Selection
nodes.detail: Choose high-utility academic words (Tier 2) that recur across texts and essential topic terms (Tier 3); model pronunciation, syllable structure, and student-friendly explanations.

nodes.label: Morphological Analysis (Roots & Affixes)

nodes.label: Semantic Networks & Multiple Contexts

nodes.label: Oral & Written Application
nodes.detail: Require active production through structured academic discussions, justification prompts, and content-area writing so vocabulary shifts from receptive recognition to expressive mastery.

diagrams.title: Reading Fluency Bridge: Accuracy, Automaticity, and Prosody to Comprehension
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Explain how accurate decoding, automatic word recognition, and syntactic prosody free working memory so elementary readers can focus cognitive resources on comprehension.
diagrams.caption: An original conceptual bridge showing how decoding accuracy, word-recognition automaticity, and expressive syntactic phrasing link foundational word reading to meaning-making.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right bridge from accurate decoding to automatic word recognition, syntactic phrasing and prosody, and freed cognitive capacity for reading comprehension.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, accurate word decoding ensures students read printed words correctly without guessing or omitting endings. Second, guided oral practice builds automatic word recognition so words are retrieved quickly with minimal conscious effort. Third, expressive prosody groups words into meaningful syntactic phrases using punctuation, stress, and intonation. Finally, because word recognition runs automatically and phrasing mirrors spoken grammar, cognitive capacity is freed in working memory for inference, monitoring, and deep comprehension.
textEquivalent: Accurate Word Decoding: Students apply reliable phonics and word-analysis skills to read words accurately in connected text, correcting miscues that would distort meaning.

Automatic Word Recognition: Through repeated reading, echo reading, and wide connected practice, students shift from labored sounding out to rapid, effortless recognition of familiar orthographic patterns.
Syntactic Phrasing and Prosody: Readers chunk text into natural grammatical phrases with appropriate pitch, stress, volume, and pauses guided by punctuation and sentence syntax.

Cognitive Capacity Freed for Comprehension: Effortless word recognition and meaningful phrasing release limited working memory so readers can integrate background knowledge, draw inferences, and monitor understanding.

nodes.label: Accurate Word Decoding
nodes.detail: Reliable phoneme–grapheme decoding and self-correction keep word-reading accuracy high (typically >=95% for instructional connected text) so meaning is not derailed by miscues.

nodes.label: Automatic Word Recognition
nodes.detail: Guided oral reading (choral, echo, partner, and purposeful repeated reading) accelerates effortless word retrieval rather than encouraging rushed speed without meaning.

nodes.label: Syntactic Phrasing & Prosody
nodes.detail: Readers group words into grammatical phrase boundaries and adjust pitch, stress, and pauses to match punctuation, dialogue, and sentence structure.

nodes.label: Cognitive Capacity for Meaning
nodes.detail: When word recognition requires minimal conscious attention, working memory is freed to connect ideas across sentences, generate inferences, and self-monitor comprehension.

diagrams.learnerPurpose: Synthesize the Simple View of Reading and Scarborough Reading Rope to plan integrated K–6 close-reading lessons, diagnose instructional bottlenecks, and align flexible small-group supports.
diagrams.caption: An original elementary synthesis flow illustrating how automatic word recognition and rich lexical quality converge during close reading, guide reading-profile disaggregation, and direct MTSS small-group alignment.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right integration model linking word recognition automaticity and lexical quality to integrated close reading, reading-profile disaggregation, and flexible MTSS grouping.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, word recognition and automatic fluency reduce cognitive load so elementary students do not spend all working memory on decoding. Second, vocabulary depth, lexical quality, syntax, and background knowledge drive language comprehension. Third, both strands weave together during integrated close-reading routines combining meaning-focused fluency practice, think-aloud comprehension modeling, and text-anchored vocabulary talk. Fourth, pairing fluency metrics with reading and listening retells disaggregates student profiles to locate exact word-level or language bottlenecks. Finally, flexible needs-based grouping and MTSS dosage intensification address each bottleneck while maintaining scaffolded grade-level text access.
textEquivalent: Word Recognition and Automatic Fluency: Accurate decoding and rapid sight recognition lower cognitive load so working memory remains available for meaning making.

Vocabulary Depth and Lexical Quality: High-quality word representations linking phonology, orthography, morphology, and rich semantics combine with syntax and background knowledge to power language comprehension.
Integrated Close-Reading Routines: Classroom lessons unite meaning-focused fluency practice, teacher think-aloud modeling, and text-anchored vocabulary discussion around complex elementary texts.
Reading Profile Disaggregation: Pairing oral reading fluency checks with reading and listening retells separates word-reading deficits from language-comprehension or mixed bottlenecks.
Flexible Grouping and MTSS Dosage Alignment: Teachers form needs-based groups, scaffold grade-level texts, intensify MTSS instructional dosage when needed, and track cross-skill growth over time.

diagrams.title: Literary & Informational Text Comprehension Instruction & Breakdown Analysis
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Connect story grammar and central-idea structures, reciprocal teaching, UDL discussion scaffolds, comprehension-breakdown analysis, and gradual strategy fading for K–6 readers.
diagrams.caption: An original elementary comprehension workflow tracing explicit genre modeling and reciprocal teaching through UDL talk scaffolds, retell error analysis, and independent transfer.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right elementary comprehension cycle from story grammar and central idea through reciprocal teaching, UDL talk scaffolds, and retell breakdown analysis to gradual strategy fading.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, explicit instruction clarifies narrative story grammar elements and informational central ideas with supporting details so K–6 students anchor literal and inferential meaning. Second, teachers model reciprocal teaching routines—predicting, questioning, clarifying, and summarizing—paired with text-dependent questions on author craft and perspective. Third, UDL text-access supports, sentence frames, and collaborative discussion structures enable every learner to cite textual evidence. Fourth, oral and written retell rubrics plus inference-versus-recall checks diagnose where comprehension breaks down. Finally, teachers either refine explicit modeling or gradually fade prompts toward independent genre transfer.
textEquivalent: Genre Architecture: Story Grammar and Central Idea: Teach narrative elements (characters, setting, plot conflict, resolution) alongside informational central ideas, key details, and author craft to ground literal and inferential reading.

Reciprocal Teaching and Text-Dependent Questioning: Model predicting, questioning, clarifying, and summarizing while prompting students to justify inferences and perspective analyses with direct text citations.

UDL Access Supports and Collaborative Text Talk: Provide visual story maps, main-idea organizers, audio or glossary options, and discussion sentence frames so all K–6 learners participate in rigorous text talk.

Comprehension Breakdown and Retell Analysis: Compare literal recall against inferential reasoning using oral and written retell rubrics and text-evidence citation checks to locate exact comprehension obstacles.

Gradual Strategy Fading and Independent Transfer: Systematically reduce teacher prompts as monitoring and evidence citation stabilize so students transfer comprehension skills independently across literary and informational genres.

diagrams.title: Expository Text Structure, Elementary Inquiry, & Digital Source Evaluation Workflow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Guide elementary students through prior-knowledge checks, expository text-structure navigation, digital credibility think-alouds, organizer-based note-taking, and cross-text research synthesis.
diagrams.caption: An original K–6 inquiry and digital-literacy workflow linking knowledge activation and expository structure analysis to source credibility checks, organized notes, and cross-text synthesis.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right inquiry workflow from prior-knowledge activation through expository text structures, digital credibility evaluation, and graphic-organizer note-taking to cross-text synthesis.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, teachers check prior knowledge, surface misconceptions, and help elementary learners frame focused content-area inquiry questions. Second, explicit instruction in expository text structures, signal words, and print or digital text features guides purposeful navigation. Third, source-evaluation think-alouds model age-appropriate credibility checks across print and digital sources. Fourth, students extract and sort verified facts into structure-matched graphic organizers using multimodal research scaffolds. Finally, cross-text synthesis rubrics and milestone checkpoints confirm accurate integration and build durable background knowledge for future inquiry.
textEquivalent: Prior-Knowledge Check and Inquiry Framing: Activate relevant domain knowledge, uncover misconceptions early, and co-construct focused elementary research questions.

Expository Text Structures and Features: Model signal words for cause-effect, compare-contrast, sequence, problem-solution, and description alongside print and digital features such as headings, charts, and glossaries.
Digital Source Credibility Think-Alouds: Explicitly demonstrate how to audit authorship, purpose, accuracy, and corroboration across accessible print and digital resources.
Graphic-Organizer Synthesis and Guided Note-Taking: Support students with structure-aligned graphic organizers and multimodal scaffolds to record paraphrased facts without copying verbatim.
Cross-Text Synthesis and Milestone Checkpoints: Evaluate text-structure summaries and cross-text synthesis rubrics at planned checkpoints to support content-area inquiry transfer.

diagrams.title: Classroom Literacy Assessment & Differentiated Instruction Loop
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Apply universal screening, diagnostic error analysis, targeted small-group explicit modeling, and progress monitoring to regroup K–6 learners and collaborate responsibly within classroom teacher boundaries.
diagrams.caption: An original elementary classroom decision loop linking universal screening and diagnostic error analysis to explicit small-group teaching, progress monitoring, and flexible regrouping.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right classroom assessment loop from universal screening and diagnostic error analysis to targeted small-group modeling, progress monitoring, and flexible regrouping with team collaboration.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the elementary teacher reviews universal screening data and conducts diagnostic error analysis on decoding, oral reading fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension work to pinpoint specific skill needs. Second, the teacher delivers targeted small-group explicit modeling with scaffolded practice matched to those needs. Third, brief curriculum-based progress monitoring checks whether each learner is closing the skill gap. Finally, the teacher adjusts flexible groups and collaborates with families and multidisciplinary school team members when persistent needs exceed general classroom support.
textEquivalent: Universal Screening and Diagnostic Error Analysis: Review benchmark screening indicators and follow up with targeted phonics surveys, oral reading miscue analysis, and retell checks to isolate exact instructional needs.

Targeted Small-Group Explicit Modeling: Form skill-based small groups for explicit I-Do, We-Do, You-Do modeling, immediate corrective feedback, and scaffolded access for multilingual and diverse elementary learners.
Frequent Classroom Progress Monitoring: Administer brief, aligned mastery checks and curriculum-based measures to track accuracy, rate, and comprehension growth over time.

Flexible Regrouping and Multidisciplinary Collaboration: Update group membership as skills are mastered, share clear progress updates with families, and collaborate with multidisciplinary school teams within classroom teacher boundaries when intensive evaluation or support is warranted.

diagrams.title: Strategic Comprehension & Reading–Writing Integration Cycle
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Connect knowledge-rich reading comprehension and text-structure analysis directly to source annotation, paraphrasing, and structured elementary writing and revision.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow demonstrating how elementary reading comprehension and written expression reinforce one another from text-structure activation through source-based drafting and revision.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right reading-writing integration cycle from background knowledge and text structure through text-dependent questioning and source annotation to structured drafting and revision.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, teachers activate and build essential topic background knowledge while previewing narrative or informational text structures. Second, students answer text-dependent questions, monitor understanding, and synthesize section gists. Third, learners annotate key text evidence and paraphrase main ideas into graphic organizers rather than copying verbatim. Finally, writers use genre-aligned graphic plans and mentor sentences to draft, revise for clarity and evidence, and edit conventions.
textEquivalent: Background Knowledge and Text Structure: Teachers build necessary domain context and highlight narrative story grammar or informational structures (cause-effect, compare-contrast, sequence, problem-solution) before and during reading.
Text-Dependent Questioning and Gist Synthesis: Students respond to literal and inferential text-dependent prompts, self-monitor breakdowns, and state concise section gists in their own words.
Source Annotation and Paraphrasing: Learners underline relevant text evidence, note signal words, and paraphrase key facts into structured graphic organizers to bridge reading and planning.

Structured Drafting and Revision: Writers compose opinion, informational, or narrative pieces using planned evidence, then revise organization, word choice, and sentence fluency before editing spelling and conventions.

diagrams.title: Developmental Spelling, Sentence Construction, Conventions, & Writing Assessment Cycle
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Link qualitative spelling inventories, pattern-based word sorts, explicit sentence combining, contextualized grammar editing, and reliable writing CBM monitoring for elementary writers.
diagrams.caption: An original K–6 written-expression cycle connecting developmental spelling diagnostics and word sorts to sentence construction, contextualized editing, and psychometrically sound writing progress monitoring.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right elementary writing cycle from developmental spelling inventories through word sorts, sentence combining, and contextualized editing to writing CBM progress monitoring.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, qualitative spelling inventories determine each elementary writer's developmental spelling stage and target orthographic features. Second, pattern-based word sorts and encoding practice build automatic spelling control. Third, explicit sentence combining, expansion, and syntax frames increase sentence variety while reducing transcription overload. constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Kindergarten phoneme segmentation
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Analyze this kindergarten student's phonological and early spelling profile. (1) Identify the narrowest controlling phonemic awareness need supported by the evidence, separating oral segmentation from print knowledge. (2) Describe an explicit oral-to-encoding routine—with modeling, guided practice, tactile scaffolds, and classroom access supports—that builds full CVC phoneme segmentation without conflating spoken sounds with printed letters. (3) Justify why this match fits the student's readiness and specify brief progress-monitoring evidence showing transfer to CVC spelling.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A kindergarten student identifies rhyme and blends two-part compound words but represents only initial consonants when attempting CVC spelling. In a spoken segmentation probe, the student gives the first sound and then repeats the whole word. Letter-name knowledge is secure for most uppercase and lowercase letters, and oral vocabulary and story retell are age appropriate. The class has received daily instruction in rhyme, syllables, onset-rime, and basic letter sounds. The teacher must determine the narrow next target, describe an explicit routine that does not confuse a spoken-sound task with a printed-word task, connect the work to encoding, and state what brief evidence would demonstrate progress.
taskParts: Pinpoint the narrowest phonemic-awareness need in the kindergarten profile, separating oral segmentation from print knowledge.
Design an explicit oral-to-encoding CVC routine with modeling, guided tactile practice, and kindergarten classroom access supports.
Justify the instructional match to the student's readiness and specify brief progress-monitoring evidence of CVC spelling transfer.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Cite secure rhyme, compound blending, letter names, and story retell alongside partial initial-sound segmentation and initial-consonant-only CVC spelling.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Target full three-phoneme oral CVC segmentation using continuous-sound words, modeling Elkonin boxes with plain counters before linking sounds to letters.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Keep spoken-phoneme work distinct from print recognition, embed brief small-group practice in kindergarten literacy, and protect full story participation.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring
planningFrame.guidance: Administer a brief weekly 5-to-8-word oral CVC segmentation and dictated spelling check with a clear accuracy criterion to fade counters or reteach.

successCriteria: Pinpoints full three-phoneme CVC segmentation as the narrowest next need, distinguishing secure rhyme, compound blending, and letter names from sound gaps.
Sequences an explicit modeling, guided-practice, and application oral routine with neutral counters first, separating spoken sounds from printed letters.
Connects oral segmentation directly to guided CVC encoding using known letter-sound correspondences while preserving grade-level kindergarten story access.
Defines a brief, construct-matched oral segmentation and CVC spelling check with a clear decision rule, avoiding any clinical diagnosis or score prediction.
commonPitfalls: Reteaching rhyme, compound blending, or letter names when the kindergarten data already show those early foundational skills are secure.
Using printed letter tiles during initial oral segmentation, which blurs spoken-phoneme awareness with print recognition too early.
Listing "Elkonin boxes" without detailing teacher modeling, continuous-sound word selection, guided practice, and transition to CVC encoding.
Pulling the student from grade-level story read-alouds or making a formal clinical diagnosis from one kindergarten spelling probe.
sampleOutline: Evidence: secure rhyme, compound blending, letter names, and retell versus initial-sound-only oral segmentation and CVC spelling.
Plan: model three-phoneme oral segmentation with continuous sounds and plain counters, guide practice, then map known letters to encode CVC words.
Rationale & check: protect kindergarten story access and use a weekly 5-to-8-word oral segmentation and CVC dictation check to fade counters.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: First-grade decoding and encoding
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Evaluate this first-grade student's CVC decoding, guessing, and medial-vowel spelling data. (1) Identify the controlling word-reading and encoding need evidenced by stretched blending versus connected-text guessing. (2) Propose a coordinated instructional plan linking phoneme–grapheme mapping, cumulative blending, dictation, and controlled decodable text—with explicit modeling, guided practice, corrective feedback, and differentiation—while eliminating picture or context guessing. (3) Justify the instructional match and define formative checks that verify medial-vowel encoding and accurate transfer in connected reading.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A first-grade student reads VC and CVC words accurately when each phoneme is stretched but guesses from the first letter during connected reading. A spelling sample preserves the first and final consonants but omits medial short vowels. The student can orally blend and segment three-phoneme words when counters are used. Instruction has introduced five short vowels and common continuous consonants, but cumulative review and connected decodable practice have been inconsistent. The teacher needs an instructional plan that coordinates phoneme–grapheme mapping, cumulative blending, dictation, controlled text, feedback, and a progress check without relying on pictures or context guessing.
taskParts: Identify the controlling first-grade word-reading and encoding need shown by stretched blending, text guessing, and omitted medial vowels.
Plan phoneme–grapheme mapping, cumulative blending, dictation, and decodable text while eliminating picture or context guessing.
Justify why the routine fits the profile and define formative checks for medial-vowel encoding and connected-text decoding transfer.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast accurate stretched CVC decoding and counter-supported oral segmentation with first-letter guessing in text and omitted medial short vowels in spelling.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Coordinate explicit short-vowel phoneme–grapheme mapping, cumulative blending, dictation, and controlled decodable reading with sound-by-sound feedback.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Eliminate picture or context guessing prompts while keeping the student engaged in grade-level read-alouds, discussions, and supportive small-group practice.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring
planningFrame.guidance: Track medial short-vowel spelling accuracy on weekly dictated CVC words and unprompted decoding in fresh decodable text to decide review or progression.

successCriteria: Explains how stretched blending, connected-text guessing, and omitted medial vowels show fragile short-vowel orthographic mapping and inconsistent review.
Integrates phoneme–grapheme mapping, cumulative blending, dictation, and controlled decodable text with explicit modeling, guided practice, and feedback.
Replaces picture and first-letter guessing with print-focused decoding routines while maintaining access to rich first-grade oral comprehension lessons.
Specifies construct-matched formative checks for medial-vowel dictation and transfer in connected decodable reading without diagnostic or score claims.
commonPitfalls: Prompting the first grader to check pictures or guess from sentence context, which reinforces the exact first-letter guessing habit in the case.
Drilling isolated short-vowel flashcards without linking phoneme–grapheme mapping, cumulative blending, dictation, and controlled decodable text.
Treating accurate stretched CVC reading as full mastery while overlooking missing medial short vowels in spelling and inconsistent review.
Recommending easier patterned books or making a formal disability or placement decision from one first-grade decoding and spelling sample.
sampleOutline: Evidence: accurate stretched CVC reading and counter-aided segmentation versus first-letter text guessing and omitted medial short vowels.
Plan: model short-vowel mapping and cumulative blending, dictate CVC words, apply in controlled decodable text, and give sound-by-sound feedback.
Rationale & check: maintain first-grade read-aloud access and monitor weekly dictated medial vowels plus unprompted decoding in fresh text.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Second-grade multisyllabic transition
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Examine this second-grade student's transition from regular one-syllable words to multisyllabic reading. (1) Identify the primary structural word-analysis need evidenced by first-syllable guessing and uneven syllable-type recognition. (2) Outline a focused, cumulative decoding and encoding routine targeting high-utility syllable patterns and familiar affixes, detailing explicit modeling, multisensory guided practice, meaning connections, and classroom differentiation. (3) Justify how this sequence leverages the student's strong oral language and specify assessment evidence signaling readiness for more complex multisyllabic words.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A second-grade student reads regular one-syllable words accurately and spells common CVC, consonant-digraph, and silent-e patterns. In longer words, the student reads only the first syllable or inserts a guessed ending. Oral language and listening comprehension are strong. A diagnostic list shows inconsistent recognition of closed, open, vowel-consonant-e, and vowel-team syllables, while simple prefixes and suffixes are familiar in conversation. The teacher must select a small number of cumulative word-analysis targets, explain a multisensory decoding and encoding routine, connect word reading with meaning, and define evidence for moving to more complex words.
taskParts: Identify the primary second-grade structural word-analysis need behind first-syllable guessing and uneven syllable-type recognition.
Outline a cumulative syllable and affix routine combining modeling, multisensory practice, encoding, meaning links, and access.
Justify how the sequence leverages strong oral language and define evidence signaling readiness for harder multisyllabic patterns.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast secure one-syllable decoding/spelling and strong oral language with first-syllable guessing and uneven closed, open, VCe, and vowel-team recognition.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Target a narrow cumulative set first (closed syllables and familiar affixes), modeling multisensory syllable division, blending, encoding, and word meaning.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Leverage the student's strong oral language and familiar conversational affixes to anchor multisyllabic word study inside grade-level second-grade texts.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring
planningFrame.guidance: Check untaught two-syllable words with taught syllable types and affixes in isolation and connected reading before adding vowel-team multisyllabic patterns.

successCriteria: Identifies incomplete multisyllabic structural analysis—not one-syllable phonics or oral comprehension—as the primary barrier driving first-syllable guessing.
Selects a focused, cumulative sequence of high-utility syllable patterns and familiar affixes with explicit modeling, multisensory practice, and encoding.
Connects structural decoding directly to word meaning and authentic second-grade passages, leveraging strong listening comprehension and oral vocabulary.
Defines clear transfer evidence on novel multisyllabic words in isolation and text to signal readiness for harder patterns, without diagnostic claims.
commonPitfalls: Assigning one-syllable CVC or silent-e remediation when the second-grade diagnostic data show single-syllable decoding and spelling are secure.
Introducing all syllable types and affixes at once instead of sequencing a narrow cumulative set beginning with closed syllables and known affixes.
Teaching mechanical syllable division rules in isolation without connecting decoded multisyllabic words to encoding and the student's strong oral meaning.
Replacing second-grade texts with simpler one-syllable books or inferring a formal reading disorder from a single transition-stage word list.
sampleOutline: Evidence: secure one-syllable reading/spelling and strong oral language contrasted with first-syllable guessing and uneven syllable recognition.
Plan: model cumulative closed-syllable and familiar-affix chunking with multisensory blending, dictated spelling, and meaning checks in context.
Rationale & check: anchor word study in oral vocabulary and verify transfer on untaught two-syllable words before introducing vowel teams.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Fourth-grade fluency profile
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Analyze this fourth-grade student's narrative fluency, informational accuracy, and comprehension profile. (1) Distinguish the relative roles of phrasing/prosody, multisyllabic academic word analysis, topic vocabulary, and sentence-level comprehension in the student's performance. (2) Design two coordinated instructional routines—covering modeling, guided practice, connected application, and differentiation—and explain why timed rate drills alone are insufficient. (3) Justify the instructional fit and specify separate measures to monitor prosodic transfer, academic decoding, and passage comprehension.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A fourth-grade student reads a grade-level narrative with 97 percent accuracy but in a word-by-word manner with limited phrasing. The student answers literal questions accurately yet loses track of relationships across longer sentences. On an unfamiliar informational passage, accuracy falls to 93 percent at multisyllabic academic words. Listening comprehension is strong, and vocabulary knowledge is uneven by topic. The teacher must distinguish the likely fluency, word-analysis, vocabulary, and comprehension contributions, select two coordinated instructional approaches, explain why rate drills alone are insufficient, and identify separate measures for transfer and comprehension.
taskParts: Distinguish phrasing, multisyllabic academic word analysis, topic vocabulary, and sentence comprehension in the fourth-grade profile.
Design two coordinated explicit routines with modeling, guided practice, and differentiation, explaining why timed rate drills fall short.
Justify the instructional fit and specify separate measures for prosodic transfer, academic decoding, and passage comprehension.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Separate 97% word-by-word narrative phrasing and sentence-link loss from the 93% informational drop on multisyllabic academic words and uneven topic vocabulary.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Pair phrase-cued prosody and sentence-chunking instruction with morphological academic word analysis and vocabulary preview, explaining why rate drills fail.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Maintain fourth-grade narrative and informational text complexity via pre-taught domain words, modeled phrasing, and partner rereading rather than easier texts.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring
planningFrame.guidance: Use separate measures—a prosody rubric, untaught multisyllabic informational word accuracy, and relational comprehension checks—to guide support adjustments.

successCriteria: Distinguishes prosodic phrasing, sentence-level comprehension, multisyllabic academic decoding (93% drop), and uneven topic vocabulary from strong listening.
Designs two coordinated explicit routines (prosodic phrasing/syntax and morphological/vocabulary preview) and explains why timed rate drills alone fall short.
Embeds guided practice and differentiation in authentic fourth-grade narrative and informational passages without lowering grade-level conceptual demand.
Specifies separate, construct-matched measures for prosodic transfer, academic word analysis, and passage comprehension without diagnostic or score claims.
commonPitfalls: Prescribing timed speed-reading drills alone, which chase words-per-minute targets while ignoring word-by-word phrasing and sentence comprehension.
Treating the 97% narrative and 93% informational scores as one single problem instead of separating prosody from multisyllabic academic decoding.
Lowering text to easier third-grade passages rather than pre-teaching uneven topic vocabulary and modeling phrase boundaries in grade-level text.
Relying on one oral-reading-rate score to track growth instead of separate checks for prosody, untaught academic words, and relational comprehension.

Rationale & check: keep fourth-grade texts intact and track growth with separate prosody, untaught academic word, and relational checks.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Fifth-grade informational comprehension
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Review this fifth-grade class's performance on grade-level science reading and summary writing. (1) Identify the controlling informational comprehension and vocabulary needs evidenced by fact-listing and missed text structures. (2) Plan an explicit instructional sequence that builds background knowledge, models text-structure analysis and gist synthesis using headings, diagrams, and causal signals, integrates text-dependent questions and written summaries, and differentiates without replacing grade-level text with simplified fact lists. (3) Justify your approach and explain how formative evidence will guide flexible regrouping and track summary transfer.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A fifth-grade class can locate isolated facts in a science chapter but produces lists rather than coherent summaries. Students rarely use headings, diagrams, causal signal words, or paragraph relationships, and several misunderstand key domain-specific vocabulary. Oral discussion improves when the teacher previews a concept map. The teacher needs to design instruction that builds relevant knowledge, explicitly models text structure and gist, requires text-dependent questions and written synthesis, and uses formative evidence to regroup students without replacing the grade-level source with simplified facts.
taskParts: Identify the fifth-grade class's controlling comprehension and vocabulary needs behind fact-listing and ignored text structures.
Sequence background building, modeled text-structure and gist synthesis, text-dependent questions, summaries, and grade-level access.
Justify the approach and explain how formative evidence guides flexible regrouping and tracks summary transfer on new science text.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast students' literal fact-finding and stronger concept-map discussions with list-like summaries, ignored headings/diagrams/causal signals, and vocabulary gaps.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Link concept-map knowledge building and domain-vocabulary study to explicit modeling of headings, causal signals, paragraph gist, text questions, and summaries.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Preserve the full fifth-grade science chapter using annotated text features, diagram walk-throughs, causal frames, and flexible small-group differentiation.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring
planningFrame.guidance: Review weekly paragraph gists and short written summaries with a criterion checklist (causal structure, accurate domain terms, coherence) to regroup flexibly.

successCriteria: Diagnoses the class's controlling need as text-structure analysis, causal-signal use, domain vocabulary, and gist synthesis rather than literal fact locating.
Sequences explicit concept-map background building, modeled heading/diagram analysis, text-dependent questioning, and guided summary writing cumulatively.
Keeps grade-level science text complexity intact while differentiating through visual organizers, talk, and vocabulary instead of simplified fact sheets.
Explains how formative gist and summary evidence informs flexible regrouping and verifies transfer to a new science section without overclaiming.
commonPitfalls: Replacing the fifth-grade science chapter with simplified fact sheets, which removes the headings, diagrams, and causal syntax students must learn.
Focusing on literal fact-finding drills when students already locate isolated facts and need paragraph-level gist and causal-signal synthesis.
Naming a "concept map" or "graphic organizer" without explaining explicit teacher modeling of headings, diagrams, domain terms, and written summaries.
Assigning fixed ability groups instead of using weekly gist and summary evidence to regroup students flexibly across the science unit.
sampleOutline: Evidence: accurate fact locating and stronger concept-map talk versus list-like summaries, ignored headings/causal signals, and vocabulary gaps.
Plan: preview a concept map and domain terms, model heading/diagram analysis and causal gist statements, then guide text questions and summaries.
Rationale & check: keep the fifth-grade science chapter intact and use weekly causal-summary checklists for regrouping and transfer.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Sixth-grade reading–writing integration
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Analyze this sixth-grade student's source comprehension, note-taking, and explanatory writing sample. (1) Identify the primary reading–writing integration needs shown by verbatim copying, unattributed notes, weak focus, and flat transitions. (2) Design an explicit instructional routine integrating purposeful annotation, paraphrasing, source tracking, controlling-idea organization, sentence combining, drafting, and revision—detailing modeling, guided practice, differentiation, and gradual release to independent writing. (3) Justify why this sequence matches the evidence and specify how you will evaluate both source comprehension and written expression.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A sixth-grade student understands two short sources during discussion but copies sentences into an explanatory response and does not organize ideas by a controlling focus. Notes mix source language, personal ideas, and uncited facts. Sentence construction is generally correct, though transitions do not show relationships. The teacher must plan an integrated routine for annotation, paraphrase, source tracking, organization, sentence combining, drafting, and revision. The response should state how explicit modeling and guided practice lead to independent writing and how the teacher will evaluate both source comprehension and written expression.
taskParts: Identify the sixth-grade integration needs shown by verbatim copying, mixed uncited notes, weak focus, and flat transitions.
Plan an explicit routine uniting annotation, paraphrasing, source tracking, controlling-idea outlining, sentence combining, and revision.
Justify why the routine matches the profile and specify how to evaluate source comprehension and written expression separately.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Distinguish strong oral comprehension of both sources and accurate basic syntax from verbatim copying, blended uncited notes, weak focus, and flat transitions.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Model and guide source-tagged annotation, oral-to-written paraphrasing, controlling-idea outlining, relational sentence combining, drafting, and revision.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Keep both sixth-grade sources central while scaffolding structured note frames, transition banks, and gradual release from joint to independent writing.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring
planningFrame.guidance: Apply a two-part rubric separating accurate source comprehension and attribution from controlling focus and logical transitions across two writing cycles.

successCriteria: Separates intact source comprehension and basic sentence control from specific needs in paraphrasing, source attribution, controlling focus, and transitions.
Integrates annotation, paraphrasing, source tracking, thesis organization, sentence combining, and revision through explicit modeling and gradual release.
Connects reading and writing authentically around both grade-level sources with differentiated note and language scaffolds that fade toward independence.
Evaluates source comprehension/attribution and written expression on distinct rubric dimensions with clear review rules, avoiding score or clinical claims.
commonPitfalls: Treating verbatim copying as poor reading comprehension or dishonesty when discussion already shows the sixth grader understands both sources.
Assigning basic sentence-grammar worksheets when sentence construction is already accurate and the real gaps are paraphrasing and logical transitions.
Telling the student simply to "put it in your own words" without modeling source-tagged notes, oral-to-written paraphrasing, and controlling-idea plans.
Grading the explanatory essay with one holistic score instead of separating source comprehension/attribution from focus and relational transitions.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Multilingual learner with strong knowledge
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Evaluate this fourth-grade multilingual learner's science knowledge, home-language strengths, and developing English literacy profile. (1) Identify the specific English academic language, morphological, and syntactic needs while distinguishing developing English proficiency from disability. (2) Propose an explicit classroom plan that preserves grade-level science access, leverages multilingual assets strategically, teaches targeted English vocabulary and sentence structures through modeling and guided practice, and offers varied response options within appropriate classroom role boundaries. (3) Justify the instructional alignment and specify progress-monitoring evidence capturing growth in both English literacy and content understanding.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A multilingual fourth grader explains complex science ideas in the home language and interprets diagrams accurately but reads English text slowly and gives short oral responses. English decoding is accurate for familiar patterns; multisyllabic words, academic morphology, and syntactically dense sentences cause difficulty. The student has received English instruction for two years and participates actively with multilingual peers. The teacher must preserve grade-level science access, use multilingual resources strategically, teach selected English language demands explicitly, provide meaningful response options, monitor growth, and avoid treating developing English proficiency as evidence of disability.
taskParts: Identify the fourth grader's English morphology, multisyllabic, and syntax needs while separating language development from disability.
Propose explicit classroom instruction preserving grade-level science rigor, strategic multilingual assets, and varied response options.
Justify the instructional alignment and define progress-monitoring checks capturing growth in both English literacy and science learning.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast strong home-language science reasoning, diagram reading, and familiar-pattern decoding with slow English reading on academic morphology and dense syntax.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Model morphological analysis of science roots/affixes and unpacking of syntactically dense English sentences, moving into guided partner talk and written claims.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Preserve fourth-grade science rigor using strategic bilingual glossaries, multilingual peer previews, diagram anchors, and varied response modes within role limits.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring
planningFrame.guidance: Track science conceptual growth and targeted English morphology/syntax transfer on separate formative checks while honoring two years of English development.

successCriteria: Identifies English academic morphology, multisyllabic terms, and dense syntax as language targets while separating two-year English development from disability.
Details explicit modeling and guided practice in morphological word study and sentence unpacking anchored directly in grade-level fourth-grade science texts.
Leverages home-language strengths, multilingual peer collaboration, diagrams, and varied response options without diluting rigor or overstepping teacher role.
Defines separate formative evidence for science understanding and English literacy transfer without making formal proficiency, placement, or disability rulings.

Diluting fourth-grade science readings into simplified worksheets or prohibiting home-language discussion that already deepens conceptual reasoning.
Reteaching basic English phonics patterns the student decodes accurately instead of targeting academic morphology and syntactically dense sentences.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Persistent word-reading difficulty
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Examine this third-grade student's response to documented, high-fidelity phonics intervention and ongoing word-reading data. (1) Identify the persistent foundational literacy needs evidenced in phonemic manipulation, automatic word recognition, spelling, and text transfer alongside strong listening comprehension. (2) Propose intensified, error-driven classroom instruction—including explicit modeling, guided practice, and accessible grade-level content participation—while specifying appropriate collaboration within the school's multidisciplinary team and classroom teacher role boundaries. (3) Justify why neither informal dyslexia labeling nor delaying a warranted evaluation is defensible, and define progress-monitoring data to share with the team.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A third-grade student has received a documented, explicit, cumulative phonics intervention with high attendance and fidelity. Progress-monitoring data show improvement in taught single-syllable patterns but persistent difficulty with phonemic manipulation, automatic word recognition, spelling, and transfer to connected text. Listening comprehension and nonreading classroom participation are strong. The teacher must intensify instruction based on error patterns, maintain accessible content participation, collaborate through the school’s multidisciplinary process, and explain why neither an informal dyslexia diagnosis nor delaying a warranted evaluation is appropriate.
taskParts: Identify the third grader's persistent manipulation, automaticity, spelling, and transfer needs alongside strong listening comprehension.
Propose error-driven intensified instruction, accessible grade-level content participation, and multidisciplinary team collaboration.
Justify rejecting both informal dyslexia labeling and evaluation delay while specifying error-pattern data to share with the team.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Document strong listening comprehension, high-fidelity attendance, and single-syllable gains alongside persistent phonemic manipulation, automaticity, spelling, and transfer gaps.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Intensify small-group explicit teaching around exact error patterns—linking phoneme manipulation, orthographic mapping, dictation, and guided connected-text transfer.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Protect third-grade content participation through audio/read-aloud access and oral responses while collaborating promptly through the school's multidisciplinary team.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring

successCriteria: Grounds urgency in documented high-fidelity intervention data showing persistent phonemic manipulation, automaticity, spelling, and text-transfer gaps.
Plans intensified, error-driven explicit modeling and guided practice linking phoneme manipulation, encoding, and connected text rather than repeating drills.
Maintains grade-level content access and clearly defines classroom teacher collaboration boundaries within the school's multidisciplinary evaluation process.
Justifies why neither an informal dyslexia label nor delaying a warranted evaluation is defensible, specifying concrete error-pattern data for team review.

Delaying a warranted multidisciplinary evaluation despite documented high-fidelity intervention, strong attendance, and persistent transfer gaps.
Repeating the exact same single-syllable phonics drills rather than intensifying error-driven phoneme manipulation, encoding, and text transfer.
Restricting the third grader to below-grade content ideas instead of providing audio or read-aloud access that leverages strong listening skills.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Advanced reader needing depth
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Analyze this fifth-grade advanced reader's comprehension strengths, worksheet disengagement, imprecise text citation, and hurried revision. (1) Identify the controlling instructional needs for intellectual depth, evidence precision, and revision craft rather than basic skill repetition. (2) Design a feasible classroom extension plan using challenging texts, inquiry, analytical writing craft, explicit modeling of precise citation and revision, and purposeful peer collaboration—without assigning extra busywork or using the student as a substitute tutor. (3) Justify why this plan fits the student's profile and specify clear criteria and assessment evidence for monitoring growth.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: A fifth-grade student reads complex novels and informational texts accurately, quickly, and with strong recall but disengages during repetitive whole-class skill worksheets. In discussion, the student makes sophisticated cross-text claims yet sometimes cites evidence imprecisely and rushes through revision. The teacher must plan extension that increases depth, complexity, research, writing craft, and intellectual responsibility rather than assigning more of the same work or using the student as a substitute tutor. The plan should include assessment evidence, access to appropriately challenging texts, collaboration choices, and criteria for monitoring growth.
taskParts: Identify the fifth grader's controlling needs for intellectual depth, exact textual citation, and substantive revision craft.
Design a feasible classroom extension using challenging texts, inquiry, modeled citation and revision, and purposeful peer collaboration.
Justify how the plan avoids busywork or substitute-tutoring duties and specify criterion-referenced evidence to monitor growth.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Separate rapid, accurate comprehension and strong cross-text discussion claims from worksheet disengagement, imprecise textual citation, and rushed revision.

planningFrame.label: Instruction
planningFrame.guidance: Compact repetitive skill worksheets and model exact textual citation, multi-source inquiry, and criterion-based analytical revision through guided conferences.

planningFrame.label: Access
planningFrame.guidance: Provide appropriately challenging paired texts and purposeful intellectual peer collaboration without assigning extra busywork or substitute-tutoring duties.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring
planningFrame.guidance: Assess multi-source analytical drafts and revisions with explicit criteria for claim depth, exact evidence citation, and substantive revision over review cycles.

successCriteria: Identifies intellectual depth, precise textual citation, and revision craft—not basic comprehension—as the controlling needs evidenced in the fifth-grade profile.
Designs a feasible classroom extension combining curriculum compacting, complex cross-text inquiry, and explicit modeling of citation and revision routines.
Ensures respectful challenge through purposeful peer discourse and authentic writing craft while explicitly rejecting extra busywork or substitute-tutor roles.
Specifies transparent, criterion-referenced writing and revision evidence to monitor growth and adjust challenge without making placement or score claims.
commonPitfalls: Assigning extra packets of repetitive comprehension worksheets or using the fifth grader as a substitute tutor for classmates instead of extending learning.
Assuming fast, accurate reading means the student needs no explicit teacher instruction in precise textual citation or substantive analytical revision.
Designing an unmanageable pull-out or gifted-placement scheme instead of feasible classroom curriculum compacting and purposeful peer inquiry.
Evaluating extension work by task volume or page count rather than explicit criteria for claim depth, exact evidence citation, and revision quality.
sampleOutline: Evidence: rapid comprehension and cross-text discussion strengths versus worksheet disengagement, imprecise text citation, and hurried revision.
Plan: compact repetitive worksheets, provide complex paired inquiry texts, model exact citation and criterion-based revision, and use peer seminars.
Rationale & check: avoid busywork or substitute-tutoring roles and track analytical drafts across cycles for claim depth, citation, and revision.
