quickReference.domainLabel: Phonological and Phonemic Awareness and Emergent Literacy
quickReference.title: Phonological Continuum & Emergent Literacy
quickReference.purpose: Anchors the oral phonological-to-phonemic progression, concepts of print, and emergent oral language benchmarks for K–6 elementary classrooms.
checklist: Confirm whether the classroom task is purely auditory (phonological or phonemic awareness) or connects speech sounds to printed letters (phonics).
Pinpoint the student's exact level on the sound-unit hierarchy before jumping to phoneme deletion or substitution.
Check concepts of print and receptive-expressive oral language alongside sound manipulation in kindergarten and early first grade.
formulas: Phonological Awareness Continuum (largest to smallest unit): Word awareness → Syllable blending/segmenting → Onset-rime manipulation → Phonemic awareness.
Phonemic Awareness Complexity Ladder: Isolation (initial, final, medial) → Blending (supports decoding) → Segmenting (supports encoding) → Addition, Deletion, and Substitution.
Concepts of Print Essentials: Book orientation, print carries meaning, left-to-right and top-to-bottom directionality, return sweep, one-to-one voice-to-print match, and letter vs. word boundaries.
Alphabetic Principle Formula: Phonemic awareness + Letter-sound correspondence = Productive understanding that printed graphemes systematically represent spoken phonemes.
decisionRules: When student data show accurate rhyming and syllable clapping but inability to sound out CVC words → teach oral phoneme blending and segmenting with Elkonin boxes, then pair tokens with letters.

When student data show fluent recitation of the ABC song while pointing randomly across lines of text → explicitly model concepts of print and one-to-one voice-to-print tracking during shared reading.
When student data show mastery of initial sound isolation but errors on medial short vowels → target explicit medial phoneme isolation and segmenting with articulatory mouth cues.
When student data show limited spoken syntax and vocabulary entering kindergarten → embed daily interactive read-alouds, turn-and-talk routines, and oral storytelling alongside phonological warm-ups.
cautions: Do not confuse phonological awareness (auditory work with spoken sounds) with phonics (connecting phonemes to written graphemes).
Do not assign complex phoneme substitution or reversal drills before elementary students master blending and segmenting three-phoneme words.
Do not treat letter-name recognition alone as sufficient mastery of letter-sound correspondence or the alphabetic principle.

quickReference.title: Six Syllable Types, Ehri Phases & Structured Phonics
quickReference.purpose: Anchors systematic K–6 phonics sequences, the six English syllable types, Ehri's word-reading phases, and orthographic mapping rules.
checklist: Inspect decoding and spelling error patterns together to see whether the gap is consonant digraphs/blends, vowel patterns, syllable division, or affixes.
Verify whether the target word is fully decodable, follows a predictable syllable type, or contains an irregular part needing orthographic mapping.
Check that explicit phonics teaching moves immediately from isolated word reading into connected decodable text and dictation.
formulas: Six English Syllable Types: Closed (CVC, short vowel: cat), Open (CV, long vowel: me), VCe (silent-e long vowel: bike), Vowel Team (ai, oa, ee, oi: boat), R-Controlled (ar, er, ir, or, ur: bird), Consonant-le (ta-ble).

Ehri's Four Word-Reading Phases: Pre-alphabetic (visual logos) → Partial alphabetic (boundary consonant cues) → Full alphabetic (complete grapheme-phoneme decoding) → Consolidated alphabetic (orthographic chunks, syllables, and morphemes).

Systematic Phonics Progression: Single consonants and short vowels → Consonant digraphs (sh, ch, th) and blends (st, bl) → VCe long vowels → Vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, and diphthongs → Multisyllabic decoding and structural analysis.
Orthographic Mapping Rule: Phonemic proficiency + Explicit grapheme-phoneme alignment (including spotlighting irregular "heart" parts in high-frequency words) builds permanent sight-word memory.
decisionRules: When student data show guessing words from the first letter and picture cues (partial alphabetic phase) → shift to explicit full-alphabetic decoding through every phoneme in decodable texts.

When student data show reading "ship" as "sip" or omitting the second sound in "stop" → distinguish consonant digraphs (two letters, one sound) from consonant blends (two sounds kept distinct) using word-building tiles.
When student data show accurate single-syllable reading but stalling on multisyllabic words in grades 3–6 → teach syllable-division routines, the six syllable types, and common prefixes and suffixes.

When student data show misreading irregular high-frequency words like "said" or "was" → map the regular consonant sounds explicitly and highlight only the unexpected vowel spelling rather than drilling whole-word flashcards.
cautions: Do not recommend three-cueing or guessing from pictures and sentence context as a primary strategy for decoding unfamiliar words.
Do not conflate consonant blends (bl, tr, where both phonemes are heard) with consonant digraphs (ch, sh, th, which represent one single phoneme).
Do not teach phonics rules purely through isolated worksheets without cumulative review, encoding dictation, and decodable passage application.

quickReference.title: Vocabulary Tiers, Fluency Pillars & Accuracy Benchmarks
quickReference.purpose: Anchors Beck's three-tier vocabulary selection, the three pillars of oral reading fluency, text-accuracy thresholds, and research-backed K–6 fluency routines.
checklist: Separate word-recognition accuracy problems from slow automaticity or flat prosody before selecting a fluency routine.
Evaluate whether an unfamiliar word merits explicit Tier 2 instruction, brief Tier 3 domain definition, or morphological/context analysis.
Confirm that fluency practice uses appropriate instructional-level text and retains a clear comprehension purpose.
formulas: Three-Tier Vocabulary Framework: Tier 1 (everyday oral words: run, table) → Tier 2 (high-utility cross-curricular academic words: analyze, reluctant, contrast) → Tier 3 (low-frequency domain-specific terms: photosynthesis, denominator).
Three Pillars of Reading Fluency: Accuracy (correct word recognition) + Automaticity (effortless, appropriate rate) + Prosody (phrasing, stress, intonation, and attention to punctuation).
Oral Reading Accuracy Benchmarks: Independent level = 95–100% accuracy; Instructional level = 90–94% accuracy; Frustration level = below 90% accuracy.

Word-Learning Toolkit: Explicit student-friendly definitions + Morphological analysis (prefixes, suffixes, Greek/Latin roots) + Context clue types (definition, synonym, antonym, example) + Multiple semantic exposures.
decisionRules: When student data show 96% decoding accuracy but slow, word-by-word pacing → assign structured repeated reading, choral reading, or partner reading with prosody modeling.
When student data show rapid reading rate that ignores punctuation and yields poor recall → model expressive phrasing using phrase-cued text and comprehension check-ins.
When student data show oral reading accuracy below 90% alongside a low WCPM score → prioritize explicit phonics and word-recognition accuracy before pushing reading rate.

When student data show limited academic word knowledge across elementary units → explicitly pre-teach high-utility Tier 2 words using student-friendly definitions, semantic maps, and morphology rather than dictionary copying.
cautions: Do not equate reading fluency with fast speed-reading WCPM while ignoring accuracy, phrasing, and meaning.
Do not rely on round-robin or popcorn reading, which lowers active reading volume and heightens elementary student anxiety.
Do not ask students to memorize isolated dictionary definitions without rich context, examples, non-examples, and repeated oral and written use.

quickReference.domainLabel: Comprehension of Literary and Informational Text
quickReference.title: Simple View, Text Structures & K–6 Comprehension
quickReference.purpose: Anchors the Simple View of Reading, Scarborough's Reading Rope, literary and informational text structures, and elementary comprehension instruction.
checklist: Determine whether comprehension difficulty stems from decoding/fluency breakdown, limited background knowledge, weak academic syntax, or poor metacognitive monitoring.
Match the graphic organizer and questioning routine to the genre (literary story grammar vs. informational text structure).
Ensure elementary students actively verify claims with text evidence and transfer strategies through gradual release (I Do → We Do → You Do).
formulas: Simple View of Reading: Decoding (D) x Language Comprehension (LC) = Reading Comprehension (RC); a weakness in either factor reduces overall comprehension.
Five Informational Text Structures: Description, Sequence/Chronology, Cause and Effect, Compare and Contrast, and Problem and Solution (each cued by specific signal words and text features).

Comprehension Depth Taxonomy: Literal (explicitly stated facts) → Inferential (implied meaning linking text clues and schema) → Evaluative/Critical (judging author's craft, perspective, and source credibility).
Reciprocal Teaching & Monitoring Cycle: Predicting + Questioning + Clarifying + Summarizing, supported by explicit teacher think-alouds and Question-Answer Relationships (QAR).
decisionRules: When student data show accurate, fluent decoding paired with weak retelling of grade-level passages → build background knowledge, explicitly teach text structure, and model comprehension monitoring.

When student data show strong listening comprehension during read-alouds but low independent reading comprehension → deliver targeted decoding intervention while maintaining grade-level knowledge building orally.

When student data show students recalling isolated facts from nonfiction without grasping relationships → teach informational signal words paired with structure-matched graphic organizers (such as cause-effect chains and Venn diagrams).

When student data show accurate literal answers but blank responses on "why" or theme questions → model inferential think-alouds using QAR ("Think and Search" and "Author and Me") with text-evidence stems.
cautions: Do not drill isolated comprehension skills (such as finding main idea on random short paragraphs) while neglecting content knowledge and vocabulary depth.
Do not misdiagnose a word-recognition bottleneck as a comprehension strategy deficit.
Do not omit digital and research literacy in upper elementary grades; students must learn to use text features, locate credible sources, and synthesize information without copying.

quickReference.title: Developmental Spelling, Writing Process & K–6 Craft
quickReference.purpose: Anchors developmental spelling stages, the recursive writing process, K–6 text genres, sentence construction, and analytic writing assessment.
checklist: Analyze student writing samples separately for idea development/organization (revising) versus spelling, punctuation, and grammar (editing).
Identify the student's developmental spelling stage to select the next orthographic pattern for targeted word study.
Verify whether the assessment goal calls for an analytic rubric (trait-by-trait instructional feedback) or a holistic rubric (overall proficiency snapshot).
formulas: Developmental Spelling Stages: Precommunicative (random letters/scribbles) → Semiphonetic (initial/final consonant cues) → Phonetic (each heard sound represented) → Transitional (visual vowel patterns and chunks) → Conventional (correct orthography and morphology).

Recursive Writing Process: Prewriting (brainstorming/planning) → Drafting (getting ideas down) → Revising (improving ideas, organization, voice, word choice) → Editing (correcting spelling, capitalization, punctuation, usage) → Publishing.

Core K–6 Writing Genres: Narrative (characters, setting, sequenced events, resolution), Informative/Explanatory (topic, facts, text features, concluding statement), and Opinion/Argumentative (claim, reasons, evidence, linking words).
Reading–Writing Reciprocity Rule: Encoding reinforces phonemic segmentation and phonics patterns, while analyzing mentor texts teaches sentence variety, genre structure, and audience awareness.
decisionRules: When student data show invented spellings like "TRN" for "train" or "BIK" for "bike" → recognize phonetic-stage mastery of consonants and teach long-vowel VCe and vowel-team word sorts.
When student data show disorganized paragraphs with weak transitions alongside spelling mistakes → conduct a revision mini-lesson on structure and clarity before moving to conventions editing.
When student data show repetitive simple sentences ("I saw a dog. It was brown. It ran fast.") → model explicit sentence combining using adjectives, appositives, and conjunctions.
When student data show a need for targeted writing conference goals across multiple traits → score drafts with an analytic rubric paired with one focused revision or editing target.
cautions: Do not conflate revising (substantive changes to content, organization, and clarity) with editing (surface corrections to mechanics, spelling, and punctuation).
Do not mark every single mechanical error on an early draft, which overwhelms elementary writers and suppresses idea generation.
Do not postpone meaningful composition in kindergarten and first grade until handwriting and conventional spelling are fully mastered.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Conflating Phonemic Awareness with Phonics
misconceptionFamilies.description: Treating oral-only phoneme tasks (blending, segmenting, deleting, or substituting spoken sounds) as print-based phonics, or introducing complex phoneme manipulation before K–2 students secure larger phonological units such as words, rhymes, syllables, and onset-rime.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Check whether print or letters appear in the task before selecting an activity: keep phonemic awareness strictly auditory-oral until students map sounds to graphemes in phonics, and sequence instruction from larger units to individual phonemes.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Three-Cueing Guessing Instead of Orthographic Mapping
misconceptionFamilies.description: Prompting K–6 beginning readers to rely on pictures, first-letter guessing, or sentence context instead of decoding through the full grapheme-phoneme sequence, or drilling irregular high-frequency words as unanalyzed visual shapes rather than mapping regular letter-sound parts.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Require eyes-on-print decoding from left to right using taught phonics patterns and decodable text, use context only to verify meaning after decoding, and teach irregular high-frequency words by mapping predictable sounds while explicitly flagging the irregular spelling part.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Equating Oral Reading Fluency with Speed Alone
misconceptionFamilies.description: Treating timed reading rate (WCPM) drills or unmonitored silent reading as complete fluency instruction while overlooking decoding accuracy, expressive phrasing (prosody), and comprehension monitoring—or prescribing speed practice when accuracy errors are the real bottleneck.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Evaluate accuracy, automatic rate, and prosody together; repair underlying decoding gaps before pushing rate, and pair modeled expressive reading or partner repeated reading with a brief comprehension check.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Isolated Dictionary Definitions Instead of Morphological and Contextual Vocabulary
misconceptionFamilies.description: Assigning dictionary copying, single-exposure weekly word lists, or unsupported context guessing for Tier 2 and Tier 3 elementary words instead of combining student-friendly definitions, rich multiple-context practice, semantic mapping, and morphological analysis.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Teach high-utility Tier 2 words and key disciplinary Tier 3 terms through explicit explanations, repeated use in speaking and writing, semantic connections, and explicit breakdown of prefixes, suffixes, base words, and roots.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Generic Comprehension Drills Without Text Structure or Background Knowledge
misconceptionFamilies.description: Teaching comprehension strategies such as finding the main idea or making predictions as isolated worksheets detached from topic knowledge, literary or informational text structures, syntax, and collaborative text-based discussion.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Anchor every comprehension routine in coherent content-rich texts, explicitly model how narrative elements or informational text structures organize ideas, and require text-grounded evidence during discussion.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Confusing Screening with Diagnostic Data and Isolating Writing Conventions
misconceptionFamilies.description: Using a brief universal screening score to choose specific skill lessons without diagnostic follow-up, or reducing elementary writing instruction and scoring to spelling and punctuation fixes while overlooking sentence craft, genre organization, and source-based evidence.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Separate assessment roles (universal screener → diagnostic skill probe → progress monitoring) and evaluate elementary writing across both transcription conventions and compositional clarity tied directly to classroom reading.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Separate Auditory Phoneme Work from Print-Based Phonics in K–2
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An item asks for a phonemic awareness task or emergent-literacy next step, yet one distractor uses letter tiles, flash cards, or worksheets—or jumps straight to phoneme deletion when a child still struggles with syllables or onset-rime.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Can a K–2 child complete this task with eyes closed using only spoken sounds, and does the sound unit match the child's exact point on the phonological continuum?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Scan the stem for two boundaries: whether letters/print are present and which spoken unit (word, syllable, onset-rime, or phoneme) the student missed.
stages.requiredOutput: State whether the target skill is phonological awareness, phonemic awareness, or phonics, and flag any distractor that injects print into an oral-only prompt.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Place the student's error on the K–2 continuum (word → rhyme/syllable → onset-rime → phoneme isolation → blending/segmenting → manipulation) and explain why print enters only at the alphabetic-principle bridge.
stages.requiredOutput: Write a two-line rule distinguishing oral phoneme blending/segmenting from grapheme-phoneme phonics decoding.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Classify three K–1 activities—clapping syllables in "butterfly," tapping three spoken sounds in "ship" with blank counters, and reading CVC word cards—by skill domain and developmental order.
stages.requiredOutput: Map each activity to phonological awareness, phonemic awareness, or phonics and justify the progression from easiest to hardest.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-read a K–2 emergent-literacy scenario where a child blends spoken onset-rime accurately but cannot segment four-phoneme blends, then select the targeted instructional move.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose the exact oral phoneme-segmentation scaffold (such as Elkonin boxes with blank tokens before adding letters) and rule out print-only distractors.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Three-Cueing Guessing Instead of Orthographic Mapping
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Replace Picture Guessing with Full-Word Decoding and Orthographic Mapping
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A K–3 student misreads a word as a meaning-similar substitute (such as reading "pony" for "horse"), and distractors suggest looking at the illustration, skipping the word, or memorizing sight-word outlines.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this instructional prompt direct the elementary student's eyes through every grapheme-phoneme correspondence in the word before checking meaning?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Identify distractors built on three-cueing habits (picture cues, contextual guessing before decoding, predictable leveled books, or whole-word shape memorization).
stages.requiredOutput: Underline the specific guessing cue in the trap option and name the decoding evidence the student actually needs to inspect.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Contrast three-cueing with orthographic mapping: bonding a word's spoken phonemes to its written graphemes and meaning in memory, including isolating the regular and irregular parts of words like "said."
stages.requiredOutput: Write a short teacher corrective prompt that guides a child to decode all sounds first and then cross-check whether the decoded word makes sense.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Plan a two-minute routine for teaching a regular decodable pattern (such as vowel team "ai") alongside one irregular high-frequency word ("does") using sound-letter mapping and decodable text.
stages.requiredOutput: List the exact phoneme-grapheme mapping for "does" (/d/→d, /u/→oe irregular part, /z/→s) and explain why decodable text reinforces the new pattern.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Apply the decoding-first rule to a new classroom scenario where a second grader reads "house" for "home" and context conflicts with print.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the response that directs attention to the medial and final graphemes, verifies pronunciation with meaning, and rejects picture-guessing distractors.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Equating Oral Reading Fluency with Speed Alone
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Balance Accuracy, Automaticity, and Prosody in Elementary Fluency
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A fluency prompt shows a student with choppy phrasing or below-benchmark WCPM, and distractors push racing a timer, silent independent reading, or round-robin popcorn reading without addressing accuracy or phrasing.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is the student's fluency breakdown driven by word-reading accuracy, slow automaticity, or flat phrasing—and does the chosen practice connect fluent reading to comprehension?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the student's oral-reading data for accuracy percentage, WCPM rate, and prosody markers (pausing at punctuation, phrasing, and intonation) to spot speed-only traps.
stages.requiredOutput: Diagnose whether accuracy (below 95% instructional threshold), rate, or prosody is the primary constraint in the vignette.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Link the three fluency pillars—accuracy, automaticity, and prosody—to comprehension, and note why unguided silent reading and round-robin reading fail to build fluency for struggling elementary readers.
stages.requiredOutput: State the decision rule: accuracy gap → explicit phonics/decoding first; accurate but slow/choppy → modeled choral, echo, or repeated reading with phrase cues and a meaning check.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Compare two third-grade profiles: Student A reads 58 WCPM with 87% accuracy; Student B reads 64 WCPM with 98% accuracy in monotone word-by-word phrasing.
stages.requiredOutput: Assign a distinct, evidence-based classroom routine to Student A and Student B, plus one progress-monitoring check that tracks both level and slope.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-evaluate a multi-week fluency progress graph and choose the defensible instructional adjustment when WCPM rises but comprehension stays flat.
stages.requiredOutput: Explain why phrasing-focused repeated reading and meaning verification outperform speed-only timed drills on the transfer item.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Isolated Dictionary Definitions Instead of Morphological and Contextual Vocabulary
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Build Deep Elementary Vocabulary with Morphology and Rich Contexts
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A vocabulary item describes upper-elementary students struggling with academic words across science or literature, and distractors recommend copying glossary definitions, memorizing 20 words on Monday, or guessing solely from vague context.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this routine give students explicit meaning, multiple active encounters in speech and writing, and transferable word-part tools (prefixes, suffixes, roots)?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot low-yield vocabulary distractors: dictionary lookup in isolation, single-exposure matching quizzes, or context-only guessing when surrounding sentences are non-directive.
stages.requiredOutput: Name the specific weakness of the isolated-definition distractor and identify the word tier (Tier 1, Tier 2, or Tier 3) targeted in the item.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Combine direct vocabulary instruction (student-friendly explanations, examples/non-examples, semantic gradients) with generative morphology (analyzing affixes and roots) and explicit context-clue verification.
stages.requiredOutput: Produce a three-part elementary vocabulary frame: student-friendly meaning → morphological breakdown → active student sentence or comparison.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Analyze the Tier 2 word "unpredictable" and the Tier 3 science term "evaporation" for a fourth-grade class that includes Spanish-speaking multilingual learners.
stages.requiredOutput: Break each word into morphemes, note one cognate or semantic connection, and write one interactive student prompt requiring deep word processing.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a fresh scenario where fifth graders read an informational passage with unfamiliar multisyllabic words and limited local context clues.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the combined morphological-analysis and teacher-clarified context strategy and explain why dictionary-copying options fail.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Generic Comprehension Drills Without Text Structure or Background Knowledge
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Ground K–6 Comprehension in Text Structure and Topic Knowledge
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A comprehension question shows students who decode accurately but struggle to summarize or infer meaning from an informational or literary passage, and distractors offer isolated "skill-of-the-week" worksheets on random short snippets.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this lesson activate or build essential topic knowledge and teach how the text's structure organizes ideas rather than drilling a generic strategy in a vacuum?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Identify distractors that treat comprehension strategies (main idea, predicting, sequencing) as content-free drills disconnected from text complexity, genre structure, or background knowledge.
stages.requiredOutput: Distinguish what the student is missing—topic vocabulary, text-structure awareness, or sentence-level cohesion—from generic strategy labels.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Pair coherent knowledge-building text sets with explicit modeling of narrative story grammar or informational structures (cause-effect, compare-contrast, problem-solution, sequence) and text-dependent questioning.
stages.requiredOutput: Outline how a teacher moves from brief background activation → explicit signal-word and structure modeling → text-evidence discussion.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Design a focused comprehension scaffold for a third-grade cause-and-effect science text on watershed erosion where students list random facts instead of explaining why erosion happens.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify the graphic organizer matched to cause-and-effect, two text-dependent questions, and one sentence-level cohesion check (such as tracking pronouns or "consequently").

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Return to a literary comprehension item where fourth graders miss a character's motivation despite fluent reading and choose the highest-leverage instructional move.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the option integrating story-grammar analysis, key inference cues, and collaborative text-based evidence while rejecting generic main-idea worksheets.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Confusing Screening with Diagnostic Data and Isolating Writing Conventions
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Match Assessment Purpose and Integrate Elementary Reading-Writing Instruction
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An assessment or writing prompt invites you to group students for specific phonics or writing lessons straight from a single universal screener, or to red-pen spelling errors without teaching sentence structure, genre moves, or source evidence.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Are we using the right assessment type for the instructional decision (screener vs. diagnostic vs. progress monitoring) and separating writing mechanics from idea organization?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Check whether the scenario misuses a broad screening benchmark to diagnose exact skill deficits or conflates transcription skills (handwriting, spelling, punctuation) with composition quality.
stages.requiredOutput: Label both the intended assessment purpose and the specific writing dimension (transcription vs. composition) described in the prompt.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Map the assessment workflow (universal screener flags risk → diagnostic probe pinpoints subskills → progress monitoring tracks response) and connect explicit writing routines (sentence combining, mentor genres, evidence use) back to reading.
stages.requiredOutput: Write one diagnostic follow-up rule for reading/writing risk and one rubric split separating conventions from content/organization.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Review a fifth-grade opinion paragraph with strong text evidence and clear reasoning but frequent spelling and comma errors, alongside a screener score placing the student below benchmark.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify the targeted diagnostic check needed for transcription, one sentence-combining/editing mini-lesson, and why you preserve the student's compositional score separately.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a new elementary scenario asking how a teacher should respond after universal screening flags four students and source-based writing drafts lack clear transitions.
stages.requiredOutput: Pick the choice that pairs diagnostic subskill follow-up with explicit genre/sentence-level writing instruction tied to classroom texts.
